title: Autonomous mobile robots for exploratory synthetic chemistry
source: Science TLDR podcast episode 14 show notes
one_line: A modular platform in which mobile robots shuttle samples between a Chemspeed ISynth synthesizer, UPLC-MS, benchtop NMR and a photoreactor, using a heuristic decision algorithm to run exploratory synthesis autonomously.
key_claims: The authors distinguish automated (human-decided) from autonomous (machine-decided) experimentation and argue automated analysis plus decision-making is what enables true autonomy.
Mobile robots link physically separated, unmodified commercial instruments, so existing lab equipment can be integrated without redesign.
A customizable, application-agnostic heuristic algorithm reads orthogonal UPLC-MS and 1H NMR data to select successful reactions, check reproducibility and direct subsequent steps.
Orthogonal UPLC-MS plus 1H NMR characterization mimics human workflows and mitigates the blind spots of any single analytical technique.

The platform is demonstrated on three distinct problems: multi-step structural diversification with medicinal-chemistry relevance, supramolecular cage/helicate discovery with host-guest binding assessment, and photocatalytic reaction screening.
limitations: Demonstrations are laboratory-scale; scaling to industrial settings is stated as future work.
Characterization relies on benchtop NMR, with high-field automated NMR noted as a needed addition for complex molecules.
Decision-making is heuristic rather than closed-loop optimization or literature/AI-informed.
Unexpected reactions or analytical results outside pre-defined criteria are not reliably handled.
No quantitative definition of 'novelty' or 'importance' exists to guide autonomous exploratory choices.
open_questions: Can the heuristic system discover a genuinely unanticipated compound or reaction class that human chemists had not pre-scoped, verified by full independent characterization?
Would swapping heuristics for closed-loop/AI-driven algorithms measurably improve hit rate per experiment on the same chemical spaces?
How much human intervention was actually required per campaign, and what is the right division of labour between robot and expert?
